items.title: Can You Use AI To Make Good Art? — With Fred Graver
items.content: Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:18 The industry is in a tailspin. There are fewer opportunities for writers and producers and people who make things. And I really had the conviction that AI can help you figure out who you are, how you have to survive in this world, and also how to make things that will then promote you and promote your career. Speaker 2 | 00:18 - 00:40 Depending on who you ask, right now is an apocalypse for creative people, or it's like the best time to be alive ever. I think it's it's one of the most important questions about AI as a technology. Can you use it to make good art, or can you only use it to make slop? That's why I'm extremely excited for this episode. My cohost Natalia Quintero interviewed Fred Graver. Speaker 2 | 00:40 - 01:03 Fred is a four time Emmy award winning filmmaker and technologist who is using AI all the time to make really great stuff in film. And he came on to share how he uses it, how it can be used as a creative tool, and the dirty secret in Hollywood that a lot of people use it even if they won't admit to it. So Natalia, tell us about the conversation. Speaker 3 | 01:04 - 01:20 It was so cool to talk to Fred and to learn from someone who's been a leader at the top of their industry for so many decades. And what's interesting is that Fred has actually done this a few times. He started his career as a Disney Imagineer. Speaker 2 | 01:20 - 01:21 That's the coolest thing. Speaker 3 | 01:21 - 02:02 Kind of the dream jobs. And then he, you know, built this incredible career at VH1 and MTV, and then he kind of threw it all away and became the head of TV at Twitter when it was a startup, and that didn't totally make sense. But he he had this really interesting thesis of wanting to get closer and closer to the audience, And now he's done it again. You know, he's basically built what will be compound producing and rebuilt the production process from the ground up using his decades of expertise, the... An Emmy award winning artist to do it all over again, and we all get to use his skills. Speaker 3 | 02:03 - 02:06 So if you want to be a producer, now you can produce like Fred. Speaker 2 | 02:06 - 02:09 I love it. It's a great episode. Let's dive in. Speaker 3 | 02:21 - 02:37 So, Fred, thank you so much for being with us. And I wanna start by actually just maybe getting a little bit of background on your career and how you got here. This... Maybe let's start, at the top. You're a professional writer. Speaker 3 | 02:37 - 02:39 Yes. How did you get into that? Speaker 1 | 02:39 - 03:04 I came to New York, and, I could type over a 100 words a minute. And we are back in the day of of IBM Selectrics and printers copies and all of that. And I went to work, and, oh, and I knew how to copy edit. And I went to work at the National Lampoon. And I was hired there, because I could I could type and I could copy edit, and I wouldn't screw up the joke. Speaker 1 | 03:04 - 03:18 So a bad copy editor would go, well, this isn't grammatically correct, and I would understand, no. That's the joke. And, I began editing, stuff at the National Lampoon and writing for the National Lampoon. So that's... Yes. Speaker 1 | 03:18 - 03:45 That's how I got started, which which for for people who are watching, who are every... In the every audience, yes, your your technical skills count. They will often get you in the door, particularly to jump ahead. You know, the whole kind of you're gonna get replaced by somebody who knows how to use AI. People who understand what's happening under the hood, are going to be incredibly in demand, I think. Speaker 1 | 03:45 - 04:09 So, I went to work from there for for David Letterman, for Late Night with David Letterman, and stayed there for a long time. It was a great gig. And then went to work for Norman Lear. In the seventies, Norman was the king of television. I think he had four or five hit shows in the top 10 of the Nielsen rankings at one time. Subscribe now How math could help alignment: …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety… AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461 ) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. items.title: Can Frontier Models See Past a Decoy? Elorian Tests Visual Reasoning
items.content: This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model , Glimpse . It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” View post on X ↗ So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount , co-released by Elorian,   provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape.  DecoyCount results Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding , co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital.   Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor , Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release , frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” How the benchmark works: “DecoyCount exposes interpretable counting failures across seven mechanisms.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were withheld from our training, and our contamination check found no overlap in the training data checked,” Dai replied, via email. “Without any cues, Glimpse scored 50.48% on the 1,660 DecoyCount items, making it the only model in the comparison to clear 50%. The closest was GPT-6 Astra at 43.17%, about 7 points behind, and Gemini-3.8-flash scored 32.71% while Qwen3.8-max scored 28.3…
items.summary: A new decoy counting benchmark exposes a gap between seeing and reasoning. Elorian’s Glimpse tries to bridge it by thinking with images.

items.title: [AINews] Gemini 4 Carbon tops leaderboards, launches for cyber defenders
items.content: It’s a good thing we published our Opus 5.5 podcast calling it the world’s best model before today’s launch. In a very pleasant surprise, Gemini announced Carbon , a newer frontier model than the 3 week old Argon , with fantastic benchmarks: Taking it to the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis consolidated benchmark, putting GDM in the lead for possibly the first time in AAII history: View post on X ↗ sd AI News for 10/27/2026-10/28/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Gemini 4 Carbon Tops Independent Leaderboards, with Access Limited to Cyber Defenders Launch : Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon two weeks after Argon. It is positioned as state of the art on cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks ( @sundarpichai , @GoogleDeepMind ). Claimed cyber results : 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for vulnerability finding, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching ( @sundarpichai ). Availability : Carbon first goes to trusted cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program, with wider developer access promised "as soon as possible" ( @GoogleAI ). items.title: Why Agents Love Supabase
items.content: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Watch the full conversation, including my opening commentary → Give the agent a backend it can read My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the applica…
items.summary: Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson on building the backend for AI agents

items.title: [AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
items.content: Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification , Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental improvements. Past guest Felix Reiseberg gets the headline today for coming out and charting the path forward for junior engineers : “ Hunger beats tenure” This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests. Enough said. His advice for juniors Pick business impact over backlog : In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Pick a radical idea : Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious! Build it over a weekend : I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype. Focus on one good idea : In my experience, junior people often make the mistake of cramming multiple ideas into a single prototype , hiding three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones. Lean into your fresh perspective : If you’re working on something user-facing, you have a unique amount of empathy for users and thus a much better sense for how the product works or doesn’t work for them. Well said, Felix! Get web search results as clean, structured Markdown, using roughly 50% fewer tokens than JSON on average. Easily integrate Markdown search results into your AI workflows across 100+…

items.title: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands
items.content: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday , the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang , heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. A model launch is also an API launch Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own produ…
items.summary: Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang on Opus 5.5, the Claude Platform, and the engineering behind AI agents.

items.title: The Manhattan Project, Take Two
items.content: In the new era of global competition, being at the forefront of Super Intelligence innovation equals geopolitical power. To maintain leadership and establish the next world order, the U.S. is moving to cement its lead. Barnett Koven is a Managing Director of AI and Data at Accenture Federal Services . He came to Accenture Federal Services after stints in industry and a faculty job at the University of Maryland, where his counterinsurgency research showed that some of the most influential quantitative studies got the answer exactly backwards. We discuss… Why “inaction is in and of itself risky” — and how government risk-aversion compounds against less-cautious competitors The “gun-armor race” in classified AI environments, where defense costs grow exponentially against linear offense Entity resolution and predictive modeling for BIS export-control enforcement, and unwrapping the PLA’s shell-company maze DOE’s Genesis Mission and Accenture Federal’s “backbone for scientific research” Thank you to Accenture Federal Services for bringing us this episode. Listen now on your favorite podcast app . From COIN to Genesis Jordan Schneider: Let’s do a bit of the career arc. How do we get from a PhD on COIN to DOE and the Genesis mission? Barnett Koven: Absolutely. I spent a lot of time in Latin America and saw the aftereffects of some virulent insurgencies in Peru and Colombia in particular, ended up doing a PhD studying the spatiotemporal diffusion of insurgent violence as a result of counterinsurgency strategy — specifically as a result of development assistance and other non-kinetic interventions during counterinsurgency. Really loved that, and sought out the opportunity to do more policy-relevant research, which is not necessarily the norm at the academy. Ended up in a faculty job at the University of Maryland, which was also wonderful — a research institution where I was encouraged and ab…

items.title: Roasting China’s AI Industry
items.content: Xianyu (咸鱼), the writer behind 葬AI — “Funeral AI” — produces some of my favorite satire about China’s AI industry. ChinaTalk readers may remember his essay “Open Models Are the United Front of AI” . In this conversation, we talk about: Why AI writing isn’t funny; How Xianyu made a website for ordinary people to rank video model by meme-ability; Why Five Year Plans are a kind of benchmark; And why there’s so much Chinglish in AI. We also disagree about where the hype is worse: China or America. The conversation is in Mandarin. Listen to the original audio here, or read a lightly abridged English translation of the transcript below. ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. On Writing Humor Irene: Xianyu, welcome to ChinaTalk. I’ve been a devoted fan since your essay on Juche AI last September, so it’s a real honor to have you here. Could you introduce yourself? When did you start writing, and how did you get into independent publishing? Xianyu: Before we begin, I just need to get it on record: Juche is a glorious ideology. I started writing Funeral AI last July or August, approaching AI through subculture. A lot of people in the AI industry maybe didn’t quite understand that. If you have a purely technical background, you may prefer very serious, professional articles. But from the beginning, I thought that even the most advanced technology — the models and APIs that frontier labs spend tens of billions of dollars developing — is available at a relatively affordable consumer price, perhaps $20 or $100. So any ordinary person has the right to describe how it feels to use AI. That was my starting point.
